title: Wassily v. Blanche: Supreme Court Weighs Green Cards After Asylum Ends - immigration-analytics.com
content:
The courtroom of the U.S. Supreme Court, where the justices hear argument Nov. 30, 2026, in Wassily v. Blanche on whether former asylees can still seek green cards. Photo: Carol M. Highsmith, Carol M. Highsmith Archive, Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division (public domain). Two men granted asylum decades ago, and later stripped of it after criminal convictions, ask the justices to decide whether “any alien granted asylum” means what it says. The Supreme Court hears argument Monday, Nov. 30, in Wassily v. Blanche, No. 25-842, a case that will decide whether a person whose asylum was terminated can still apply to become a lawful permanent resident under 8 U.S.C. 1159(b). The answer matters to every asylee whose status could be ended for a crime, a change in country conditions or fraud, and to the spouses and children whose derivative status falls with them. The case sits second on the Court’s argument calendar that morning, after Crowther v. Board of Regents. Briefing closed Nov. 2 with the petitioners’ reply, so the arguments the justices will test are now fully on paper. This site first explained the question in October; what follows is what each side has since told the Court. Tamer S. Wassily, an Egyptian Coptic Christian, entered on a visitor visa in 1993 and won asylum in 2000. After 2004 New York convictions for stalking and child endangerment, an immigration judge terminated his asylum on the ground that he had committed a particularly serious crime. On remand years later, an immigration judge again terminated asylum but granted him adjustment with a waiver. The Board of Immigration Appeals reversed, applying its 2022 precedent Matter of T-C-A-, 28 I&N Dec. 472, which holds former asylees categorically ineligible, and ordered him removed. Byron E. Velasquez Arreaga, a Guatemalan granted asylum in 1996, lost it after drunk-driving convictions and was ordered removed after his adjustment application was dismissed as ineligible. A divided Second Circuit panel sided with the government in August 2025, Wassily v. Bondi, 150 F.4th 100. Judge Richard Wesley, joined by Judge Joseph Park, held that Section 1159(b) “allows only noncitizens with current asylum status to adjust.” Judge Beth Robinson dissented. The Fourth Circuit reached the same result as the majority in Cela v. Garland (2023); the Fifth Circuit went the other way in Siwe v. Holder (2014). That split is why the Court took the case. The petitioners argue that “granted” is a past participle describing a completed event, and that “any” is a word of breadth. Congress wrote continuing conditions into Section 1159 three times, they point out, including a requirement that the applicant still be a refugee, but never wrote one requiring current asylum status. The government’s reading, they say, would also hollow out the Attorney General’s waiver authority in Section 1159(c), since an adjudicator could defeat eligibility simply by terminating first. They fall back on the rule of lenity. The Solicitor General answers that the provision speaks of adjusting a person’s “status,” which signals a present condition: the applicant must hold the first status when the adjustment happens. The benefits that come with asylum under Section 1158(c)(1) end at termination, the brief argues, and adjustment is one of them. It leans on a 1990 provision that let certain earlier asylees adjust “regardless of whether or not such asylum has been terminated,” reasoning that Congress would not have needed that language if the general rule already covered former asylees. On the waiver point, the government says an adjudicator keeps discretion because it may decide adjustment before termination, citing Matter of K-A-, 23 I&N Dec. 661 (BIA 2004). Lenity does not apply, it says, to a discretionary benefit. The regulation USCIS applies, 8 CFR 209.2(a)(1), covers “any alien who has been granted asylum” and lists conditions such as one year of physical presence and continuing refugee status, without an explicit requirement that asylum be unterminated. Expect both sides to claim that text. Asylee adjustment is a substantial pipeline. In fiscal 2023, 40,330 people adjusted to permanent residence as asylees, according to the DHS Office of Homeland Security Statistics, up from 20,550 in fiscal 2021. No public figure shows how many former asylees are waiting on this question, and none of the briefs supplies one. Families are the sharpest edge. Under 8 CFR 1208.24(d), terminating a principal applicant’s asylum automatically terminates the derivative status of a spouse or child, though they may file their own claims. If the government wins, that derivative family member loses the Section 1159(b) path at the same moment, whatever his or her own record. The National Immigrant Justice Center pressed that point in an amicus brief; immigration law professors and the American Immigration Lawyers Association also filed briefs, while the Federation for American Immigration Reform and America’s Future filed in support of the government, arguing that asylum is meant to be temporary and lenity has no role. The practical effect of a government win would be to make the order of proceedings decisive: an asylee who adjusts before termination keeps the green card path, while one whose termination comes first loses it entirely. A petitioners’ win would not guarantee anyone a green card. Applicants would still need to clear admissibility, often through a discretionary waiver, and immigration judges and the BIA would still weigh the convictions that triggered termination. The open question is how much the justices care about that sequencing problem versus the word “status,” and whether, after Loper Bright, any justice is willing to rest on the BIA’s reading in T-C-A-. Both lower courts in the majority decided the question on their own reading of the statute. The case lands as the BIA narrows other escape valves, including its Nov. 23 ruling ending equitable tolling for late appeals and its warning in Matter of K-L-S- on frivolous asylum appeals, and as researchers count more people losing temporary protections. title: Next-Gen 2028 Honda CR-V Goes Hybrid Only, and It’s a Fuel-Sipping Family SUV Worth Waiting For - Car and Driver
content: Honda’s bestseller goes hybrid only as it enters its seventh generation and will arrive in 2027 with a fresh design inside and out. Honda’s bestselling model—and the third-bestselling vehicle in the United States through the third quarter of 2026—is getting a complete makeover. The CR-V will follow the path set forth by the sixth-generation Toyota RAV4, going hybrid only as the CR-V enters its seventh generation for the 2028 model year. We expect the 2028 CR-V Hybrid to wear a sharp new design, with spy photos showing slim daytime running lights above a series of thin horizontal grilles, while the rear end features a light bar that stretches the full width of the SUV. It will likely also be the first vehicle in the U.S. to wear Honda’s new “H” logo, which was originally introduced for its future EVs but will now be applied to other vehicles in its lineup after Honda hurriedly canceled said EVs earlier this year. The cabin is also expected to get a significant makeover, with the Avancier—a three-row SUV sold in Asia—providing hints about what to expect. The Avancier skips out on most real buttons and knobs, instead putting nearly every function into a large screen mounted to the dashboard, a dramatic shift from Honda’s current setup that prioritizes physical controls. The Avancier’s interior is wrapped in white upholstery, accented by glowing ambient lighting, and features a squared-off steering wheel. Honda also appears to be switching to a column-mounted gear selector. See all results for new 2028 Honda CR-V Hybrid for sale near 23917 While Honda was once led by the Accord and Civic sedans, in today’s SUV-obsessed market, the CR-V has become the Japanese automaker’s most important model. Its biggest rival, the RAV4, was overhauled for 2026 and went hybrid only. Now, the CR-V will follow suit to stay competitive in the incredibly crowded compact SUV segment. Hybrid sales of the current-generation CR-V have been strong, accounting for over half of the SUV’s total sales so far this year, making it a perfect choice to launch Honda’s new platform and hybrid powertrain. The CR-V will arrive on a new platform that Honda promises will be stiffer and lighter than before, taking a modular approach that will lead to greater parts sharing and reducing costs. This platform will presumably be adapted to underpin future versions of the Accord and Civic, along with Acura models such as the upcoming next-generation RDX Hybrid. Honda will ditch the standard 190-hp 1.5-liter four-cylinder engine for the 2028 CR-V, which will arrive exclusively with the company’s new hybrid powertrain. The fifth generation of Honda’s two-motor hybrid setup will continue to use an Atkinson-cycle four-cylinder, along with a pair of electric motors, but the 2.0-liter engine will be a fresh design, featuring a new cooling system. As before, the electric motors will power the wheels most of the time, but the gas engine can also be engaged to directly drive the wheels. See all results for new 2028 Honda CR-V Hybrid for sale near 23917 The electric motors are more compact than before, and Honda has developed a new battery too. The company says the new hybrid setup will bring improved power and efficiency, targeting 10 percent better fuel economy than the outgoing hybrid powertrain. The current CR-V Hybrid makes 205 horsepower and is rated at up to 38 mpg combined. We wouldn’t be surprised to see power increase to over 220 hp—the RAV4 makes 226 hp in FWD form and 236 hp with AWD—and fuel economy nudge up to just over 40 mpg. The CR-V is expected to come with front-wheel drive standard and all-wheel drive optional, although it’s unclear if the latter will see the addition of a third electric motor. Honda will also likely include the S+ Shift feature seen on the Civic Hybrid and Prelude, which simulates a traditional transmission’s gearchanges and allows the driver to manually shift with the steering-wheel paddles. The CR-V’s chief rival will continue to be the Toyota RAV4. However, the Hyundai Tucson Hybrid and Nissan Rogue Hybrid, which both enter a new generation for 2027, will also be strong competitors. The Jeep Cherokee, Kia Sportage Hybrid, and Subaru Forester Hybrid will be in the mix too, along with nonhybrid compact SUVs like the Volkswagen Tiguan. The move to only offer a hybrid powertrain could see the CR-V’s entry price climb, which might alienate some buyers. Honda will also need to make sure it can match or exceed the efficiency of rivals like the RAV4 while still providing adequate performance and a spacious, usable cabin, given how closely matched the compact SUV space is these days. Moving away from physical interior controls could also upset the Honda faithful who are used to the company’s simple-to-use buttons. Production is set to kick off at Honda’s factories in East Liberty, Ohio, and Greensburg, Indiana, in April 2027. Sales should begin shortly after, and with the current CR-V Hybrid starting at $37,580, we expect the next-generation model to come in at around $38,000. title: NetChoice v. Clark (Vermont) - NetChoice
content:
Case Status: Complaint filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Vermont
Latest Update: November 24, 2026
Attorneys: NetChoice is fighting to stop the Vermont Speech Code, an attempt by the government to censor speech online and create unlawful barriers to protected speech that would jeopardize all Vermonters’ cybersecurity—especially for children—and thwart parents. Under the Vermont Speech Code, the government decides what lawful information and ideas people may access online. It conscripts websites to act as digital speech police, violating the First Amendment rights of users and service providers alike. Companies that won’t censor will effectively be forced to verify the age and identity of every Vermonter. That creates a honeypot of sensitive documents for cybercriminals and predators, at a time when children are already the top targets for identity theft. The U.K. and Australia have tried this model, and their own regulators now admit it hasn’t worked. The Vermont Speech Code also puts the state in the role of parents, overriding families’ decision-making about their children’s online experiences. Young people in non-traditional home situations, like those in foster care or informal guardianships, risk being cut off from vital information entirely. There are lawful ways to keep young people safe online without sacrificing the rights and security of all Vermonters. NetChoice’s complaint filed on November 24, 2026, in the U.S. District Court for the District of Vermont.

title: General Intent in Gambia v. Myanmar - Just Security
content:
Last week, the International Court of Justice found that the Republic of the Union of Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya ethnic group during its “clearance operations” in northern Rakhine State in 2017. The Court found that Myanmar’s security forces committed three acts listed in the Genocide Convention—killing members of a group, causing serious bodily or mental harm to members of a group, and imposing measures intended to prevent births within a group—with the specific intent to destroy a substantial part of the group. This article focuses on the Court’s distinct finding that Myanmar’s security forces committed these listed acts with general intent. As we shall see, the Court’s findings with respect to general intent provided an indispensable foundation for its findings with respect to specific intent. Genocide is a “dual intent” crime. Listed acts must be committed with both general intent and the specific intent to destroy a group in whole or in part. In simple terms, general intent involves the perpetrator’s mental state with respect to their own conduct and its direct consequences for individual victims, while specific intent involves the perpetrator’s mental state with respect to the broader consequences of their conduct for the victim group as such. Both are required. The Gambia had to show that Myanmar’s security forces killed, injured, and prevented births among individual victims with general intent, and that Myanmar specifically intended to thereby destroy a substantial part of the victims’ group. While specific intent involves the purpose or aim to bring about a result, the Court clarified that general intent is a broader concept. “Killing” must be intentional, as must “causing serious bodily or mental harm”. Mental elements are made explicit in paragraphs (c) and (d) of Article II by the words “deliberately” and “intended”, quite apart from the implications of the words “inflicting” and “imposing”; and forcible transfer too requires deliberate intentional acts. The acts, in the words of the ILC, are by their very nature conscious, intentional or volitional acts (Commentary on Article 17 of the 1996 Draft Code of Crimes against the Peace and Security of Mankind, ILC Report 1996, Yearbook of the International Law Commission, 1996, Vol. II, Part Two, p. 44, para. 5). In Gambia v. Myanmar, the Court returned to the same passage of the ILC Commentary, which continues: “[t]he prohibited acts enumerated in subparagraphs (a) to (e) are by their very nature conscious, intentional or volitional acts which an individual could not usually commit without knowing that certain consequences were likely to result” (emphasis added). the words “killing” and “meurtre” appear in the English and French versions respectively of subparagraph (a) of Article II of the Convention. For the Court, these words have the same meaning, and refer to the act of intentionally killing members of the group (I.C.J. Reports 2007 (I), p. 121, para. 186 and Blagojević and Jokić, IT‑02‑60‑T, Trial Chamber, Judgment of 17 January 2005, para. 642). In Gambia v. Myanmar, the Court picked up where it left off, citing the same ICTY Trial Chamber judgment in Blagojević and Jokić as well as ICTY Trial Chamber judgments in Karadžić and Krstić and the ECCC Trial Chamber judgment in Case 002/02 (Nuon Chea and Khieu Samphan). The Court observed that the expression “intentional killing” has been given the same meaning as “murder” within the definition of crimes against humanity in the jurisprudence of international criminal tribunals. In the Court’s view, a killing is intentional within the meaning of Article II (a) of the Convention where the perpetrator meant to cause the death of the victim or acted with knowledge that death was a likely consequence of the act or omission. This does not include negligence or gross negligence (citations omitted). Similarly, the Court found that causing serious bodily or mental harm with general intent involves meaning to cause such harm or knowing that such harm is likely to result from one’s conduct (para. 334). Finally, imposing measures intended to prevent births with general intent involves meaning to prevent births or knowing that one’s conduct is likely to prevent births (para. 369). In his Declaration, Judge Tladi writes that “the Court acknowledges, in substance, the relevance of dolus eventualis in respect of the actus reus.” The trial judgments cited by the Court found that “killing” as a genocidal act and “murder” as a crime against humanity may involve either dolus directus or dolus eventualis. In common law terms, dolus directus corresponds to direct intent or purpose, while dolus eventualis involves acceptance of foreseen risk analogous to implied malice or depraved indifference (see Stakić). While the Court does not expressly mention the dolus eventualis element of acceptance of risk (sometimes described as “reconciliation” or “consent”), the formulation it draws from the ILC (knowledge of likely results) is close if not identical in substance. The Court’s understanding of general intent is legally sound. It draws on the Court’s own prior decisions, the sources cited therein, as well as other judicial decisions by international courts and tribunals. Notably, none of the dissenting opinions take issue with it. Two prior articles examine general intent and dolus eventualis at greater length (see here and here). On a personal note, it was an honor to see the first article cited by Judge Tladi in his Declaration. On the facts, the Court found that Myanmar’s security forces intentionally killed approximately 10,000 Rohingya. According to the Court, “the killings included, inter alia, the direct targeting of civilians, including women and very young children, and killings with knives and burning of people in houses.” These acts were plainly meant to kill. The Court also found “killing by widespread indiscriminate shooting.” These acts were plainly meant to kill in the vast majority of cases, and in practically all cases were committed knowing that they would likely result in death. The Court also found that Myanmar’s security forces intentionally caused serious bodily and mental harm, including through the rape of at least 1,834 Rohingya women and girls, often accompanied by beatings or mutilation. These acts were plainly meant to cause serious bodily harm. At a minimum, these acts were committed with knowledge that they were likely to result in serious mental harm (paras. 329 & 334). Crucially, the Court found that Myanmar’s security forces intentionally caused serious mental harm through the forcible displacement of approximately 700,000 Rohingya across northern Rakhine State. Drawing on Tolimir and Karadžić, the Court found that serious mental harm can result from “violent separation from and loss of family members, the destruction of homes and the inability to return home, ongoing uncertainty regarding the fate of relatives and their whereabouts, ‘appalling conditions of the journey … by bus and on foot’, and ‘post-transfer suffering’” and that such serious mental harm was in fact caused to “a very significant number of members of the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine State.” The perpetrators of the forcible displacement may or may not have meant to cause serious mental harm to their victims. However, as the Court explained, at a minimum, [] the above violent acts were committed by the Myanmar security forces with knowledge that they were likely to result in serious mental harm to the Rohingya population. They thus constitute intentional acts. The Court’s broad understanding of general intent was apparently crucial to its finding that forcible transfer caused serious mental harm across northern Rakhine State. As we shall see, this finding was in turn crucial to the Court’s finding of specific intent. Finally, the Court found that Myanmar’s security forces imposed measures intended to prevent births within the group, primarily through widespread sexual violence. The direct perpetrators may or may not have meant to prevent births but, as the Court explained, they must have known that their acts would likely cause that result. Here, too, the Court’s broad understanding of general intent may have been decisive. The Court did not find that Myanmar’s restrictions on movement and humanitarian aid amounted to deliberately inflicting on the group conditions of life calculated to bring about its physical destruction in whole or in part under article 2(c) of the Genocide Convention. According to the Court, such conditions of life must be “objectively capable of causing the death, over time, of at least a substantial part of the protected group” as a matter of “objective probability.” The Court found that Myanmar’s restrictions on movement and humanitarian aid were not objectively capable of causing so much death on their own. The Court did not expound on the accompanying general intent requirement, but it appears to amount to (i) meaning to inflict such conditions or (ii) knowing they are likely to cause such a result. As we have seen, the Court found that the forcible displacement of 700,000 Rohingya intentionally caused serious mental harm, because the perpetrators must have known that serious mental harm would likely result. The Court did not have to find that each individual perpetrator acted with the purpose, or aim, to cause such harms, which would have been more difficult, if not impossible. It was enough to find that the perpetrators must have known that they would likely cause these results, which seems difficult to deny. The Court’s finding that forcible displacement caused serious mental harm with general intent, proved critical to the Court’s analysis of specific intent. From this premise, it followed that the entire Rohingya population of northern Rakhine State—some 800,000 people—was extensively targeted with listed acts by Myanmar, and not only those group members killed or subject to sexual violence in specific locations. This was the starting point of the Court’s ultimate finding that Myanmar specifically intended to destroy a numerically substantial part of the Rohingya group. Other important factors, including the general context of discrimination, selective targeting, attacks on women and children, and the systematic nature and scale of the relevant conduct, filled out the Court’s understanding of Myanmar’s conduct and specific intent. Notably, the dissenting judges agreed that forcible displacement is capable of causing serious mental harm (para. 56), and did not dispute the Court’s broad understanding of general intent. However, the dissenting judges found insufficient evidence that the “vast majority” of displaced Rohingya in fact suffered mental harm so serious as to result in “long-term disadvantage to a person’s ability to lead a normal and constructive life.” Instead, these judges found extreme violence concentrated in specific villages, but not targeting the Rohingya group across northern Rakhine State. Accordingly, these judges were “not at all convinced, and even less ‘fully’ convinced,” that Myanmar specifically intended to destroy the Rohingya of northern Rakhine State. This was the basic point of dispute between the Court and the dissenting judges regarding specific inent. The Court’s broad understanding of general intent is legally sound. In future cases, the Court may have to examine how this broad understanding applies to military operations directed at military objectives with knowledge that civilian harm is likely to result. As an earlier article explains, the Court may find that such military operations constitute “killing” or “causing serious bodily or mental harm” within the meaning of the Genocide Convention, but that full compliance with international humanitarian law will typically defeat an inference of specific (genocidal) intent. Alternatively, the Court may find that such military operations will typically constitute “killing” or “causing serious bodily or mental harm” within the meaning of the Genocide Convention only if they violate international humanitarian law. On the latter view, armed forces who fully comply with international humanitarian law may know their conduct is likely to cause death, but they do not “accept” (“reconcile” themselves to, “consent” to, or display “manifest indifference” toward) this result within the meaning of dolus eventualis. The Court’s resolution of such issues may prove both interesting and consequential. Adil Ahmad Haque  (Bluesky - X) is Executive Editor at Just Security. title: A.R. and Others v. Poland, H.M.M. and Others v. Latvia and C.O.C.G. and Others v. Lithuania - ECHR
content: Responding to realities of instrumentalisation of migration at Belarus border, the Court safeguards essential rights and reiterates limits of Convention protections. The Court delivered Grand Chamber judgments in the cases of A.R. and Others v. Poland, H.M.M. and Others v. Latvia and C.O.C.G. and Others v. Lithuania. In A.R. and Others v. Poland, the first applicant fell into the second category of vulnerability because on the date of his removal, an interim measure granted under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court had been in force. The Court held, unanimously, that there had therefore been a violation of Article 3 in respect of the first applicant on account of his removal to Belarus on 20 October 2021. In H.M.M. and Others v. Latvia, the Court held that the applicant children fell within the first category of vulnerability and that their adequate protection could not be ensured without the presence and support of their close family members. The Court held, unanimously, that there had therefore been a violation of Article 3 in respect of the applicant children and their accompanying family members on account of their removal to Belarus on various dates. However, in respect of the adult applicants in that case, who did not fall into either category, the Court held, unanimously, that there had been no violation of Article 3. In C.O.C.G. and Others v. Lithuania, the Court found that the applicants did not fall into either category. The Court held, by eleven votes to six, that there had therefore been no violation of Article 3. The cases of A.R. and Others v. Poland, H.M.M. and Others v. Latvia and C.O.C.G. and Others v. Lithuania concerned attempts by individuals from Afghanistan, Iraq and Cuba to enter Council of Europe member States unlawfully from Belarus in 2021 and 2022. This occurred in a context of hostile actions carried out by the Belarusian authorities referred to as “instrumentalisation of migration”, where Belarus had encouraged, facilitated, or forced the movement of migrants across its borders with the intention of destabilising the respondent States or the wider region.

title: Being the V’ - Jewish Journal
content: After a school week spent with my best friends, I look forward to spending a few hours each Saturday at shul with my other best friends — the ones who are at least quadruple my age. The time I spend with these friends at synagogue is the highlight of my week. It’s an oasis of unbridled joy, enthusiasm and lots of “puh, puh, puh”s to avoid drawing the evil eye. It’s a much-needed break from the rat race that is 10th grade, two solid hours of spiritual respite and renewal, and I’m lucky to get to experience it with the most passionate and joyous Jews around. Some Saturdays, I engage with the other end of the spectrum. Through working with my synagogue’s youngest congregants at the Shabbat childcare, I get to see the delight on each kid’s face as they exclaim the lyrics to Bim Bam and gallivant around with stuffed torahs. A girl excitedly tells me about the challah she made the previous day in preschool. A boy loudly asks another volunteer to read him “Sammy Spider’s First Passover” over and over. These two groups are both unabashedly, and proudly, Jewish. For the latter, it’s because they haven’t been taught not to live that way yet. But for the former, it’s because they’ve finally stopped listening to those who teach them not to Jew out loud, so to speak. You’re almost certainly familiar with the concept of “L’dor V’dor,” from generation to generation. Almost every week since birth I’ve sung those words, but only recently did their pertinence to my life dawn on me. I, my sisters, my friends at school—we’re the “V’”. We are the bridge between two joyous generations. Preventing said bridge from sinking into the mud of assimilation and despair hasn’t been easy these past few years, so we definitely have our work cut out for us. But how? How can we keep living joyously in our Judaism in a time where society tells us to do the opposite? The answer to this is shockingly simple: community. To witness joy is to experience joy, so by spending time with these two incredibly happy groups, we multiply our own happiness. This is possible through so many ways, like shmoozing over bagels with the Deborahs and Davids in your own community, or reading PJ Library books to little Elijahs and Mayas. At my local nursing home this summer, I taught Jewish seniors how to journal. I grew extremely close with my group of residents, and began looking forward to telling them all about my week and in turn hearing about theirs. All of our regulars were deeply happy Jews, possessing a kind of happiness that can only be experienced once you let go of the unofficial edicts of our society that tell us to be solemn and secret Jews. I came out of that experience changed, having born witness to the purest nachas out there. During the school year, I serve as an assistant teacher at my alma mater Hebrew school. I work with kids ranging from ages 5 to 12, and I see the excitement on their faces before shira (song session), tefillah (prayers), and even before the tzedakah (charity) box is passed around every week. Primary Jewish education like this cultivates the inherent joy found in kids into the basis of a strong, lifelong Jewish identity — and one rooted in elation. The Jewish spirit thrives in those too young or too old to be affected by the antisemitic ways of our world, those that try and quash the multigenerational soul that our tradition carries. Simply put, we start joyous and end joyous, but may stray from the path along the way. By amplifying the happiness these two discrete generations receive from being Jewish, we can be the bridge. As we serve as the v’, we ensure dor will become dor will become dor, for as long as time extends. Being the v’ isn’t easy. Frankly, being Jewish isn’t exactly an easy lift. But, with the right mindset and some help from friends across all ages, we can do it. We can carry on the Jewish joy of our parents and of our children. We can, and we will.
